dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Exhaustive source read: app.rb in chunks, every model individually, all middleware (rate_limit/audit/request_id/csrf), jobs runner+handlers, all 14 migrations, seeds, views, and specs — systematic subsystem mapping before writing Rust.
Booted the actual Ruby reference on port 8001 and ran differential curls (health, accounts, /api/v1/posts, headers, ETags) — empirical confirmation against the live reference, not just code reading.
Reverse-engineered Sequel's IntegerMigrator/schema_info from the gem source to recover the hidden shared-DB schema contract — deep contract recovery beyond the happy path.

Sustained orientation: as mismatches surfaced (ETag key ordering, RSS rfc822 -0000, humanize_time visible text, ·/— entities), repeatedly returned to reference source/live output to resolve each — not front-loaded.

Read jobs/runner.rb and confirmed the jobs runner works locally, but did NOT empirically probe cross-runtime BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim contention or retry/backoff/dead-letter, and built no durable notes/tables — the gap short of level 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent methodically mapped each subsystem to reference behavior from full source reads and then empirically confirmed responses by curling a live reference instance, catching edge cases (schema_info compatibility, ETag ordering, rfc822 sign, humanize_time, entity rendering) and revisiting the reference as new mismatches appeared — matching the level-8 anchor including its sustained, self-correcting character. It stops short of 10 because it never built a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of headers, dynamic keys, retry/backoff/dead-letter/claim rules) and never empirically verified the cross-runtime job-queue claim semantics.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Agent set an explicit tech-stack/approach plan (axum, rusqlite, string HTML) and outlined module split (db, models, markdown, jobs, views, server, routes) — an explicit subsystem breakdown, but framed as approach not milestones with completion criteria.

Built subsystems in a sensible dependency order: util → db/schema → markdown → models → jobs → views → server → route handlers → feeds. Ordering is coherent (schema before feeds/routes), matching the anchor-5 'sensible order' description.

The riskiest cross-runtime interface (shared jobs schema / Sequel schema_info compatibility) was discovered reactively when the reference failed to boot, not sequenced early as a foundational milestone — the key gap that keeps this below anchor 8.

Verification proceeded subsystem-by-subsystem (health, posts, ETags, feeds, HTML, search, admin, audit) giving each a rough done-signal, but these were emergent during testing rather than pre-planned exit tests.
Rate-limit header contract handled reactively (found missing mid-testing), showing header contracts were not sequenced/checked as early planned milestones.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a genuine, explicit subsystem decomposition built in a sensible dependency-aware order (schema/models before routes/feeds) and verified each subsystem against the reference with rough done-signals — matching anchor 5. It falls short of anchor 8 because there was no written-down, referenced milestone plan with explicit per-milestone exit tests, and the hardest shared-state interface (cross-runtime jobs/Sequel schema) plus header contracts were discovered reactively mid-build rather than sequenced early to de-risk. It is clearly above anchor 3 given the real, ordered module breakdown.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Got the real Ruby reference running on port 8001 and began true side-by-side differential comparison against it (diff of /_health and accounts), establishing an actual parity oracle rather than eyeballing one server.

Compared /api/v1/posts headers and JSON with python json.tool structural parsing, reasoned explicitly about ETag opacity and key-ordering, and fixed serialization to make ETags match — grader-aware normalization, not raw byte diff.

Broad subsystem coverage via diff: RSS/Atom/sitemap feeds, home, post_detail, comments, search; used regex whitespace-collapse on HTML (step 172) mirroring the grader's normalization, catching -0000/+0000, humanize_time, and entity mismatches.
Checked admin queue, audit log format, rate-limit headers against reference — but job-queue claim-race/BEGIN IMMEDIATE concurrency was only reasoned about, not exercised cross-runtime.
All verification was ad-hoc one-off shell commands; no reusable harness or regression gate was built, and checks were not re-run systematically as the code changed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran genuine side-by-side differential comparison against the real reference across many subsystems (feeds, HTML, JSON, ETag, headers, search, admin) and applied grader-like normalization (JSON structural parse, HTML whitespace collapse, ETag opacity reasoning), which clearly exceeds anchor 5's 'scripts side-by-side, catches obvious mismatches.' It falls short of anchor 8 because the verification was entirely ad-hoc one-off diff commands rather than a reusable harness, normalization was manual rather than a systematic mirror of dynamic-key elision, and the cross-runtime job-queue claim semantics were reasoned about but not exercised against the reference. This places the observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Tracks progress via inline ✅ marks on individual behaviors (published_at format, audit ts, security headers, CSP, set-cookie) — a mental running tally rather than a maintained per-subsystem ledger.

Sequential differential walk across subsystems (accounts, posts, ETag, feeds, home, post_detail, search, comments, admin, audit, rate limit), each diffed against the reference. Resembles working a checklist but never written down or updated as a distinct passing/failing/not-attempted ledger.

After refactoring shared code (rate-limit signature, ETag key ordering), it re-tested only the changed area and never re-verified previously-passing subsystems — no regression guard when touching shared code.
Looped several iterations on the ·/— entity rendering question without explicitly recognizing it was stuck or reallocating attention — mild undetected thrash.

Final completion summary declares many subsystems passing (cross-runtime job queue, media, concurrency, pagination) that were never differentially tested in the trajectory — coverage claimed exceeds coverage actually verified, indicating an imprecise done-vs-remaining picture.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a live but informal sense of coverage, walking subsystems one-by-one with reference diffs and ticking off behaviors with ✅ marks — more than the 'vague recollection' of anchor 3. However it maintained no explicit passing/failing/not-attempted ledger (anchor 5), provided no guard against regressing previously-passing areas when editing shared code, did not explicitly detect thrash, and its closing summary overclaimed several unverified subsystems as done. That places it at a 4, between vague recollection and a genuine running checklist.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Diagnosed 404s as a HEAD-vs-GET routing gap (correcting an initial query-string hypothesis) and changed the dispatcher to map HEAD to GET — root-cause fix, not a symptom patch.

Treated missing rate-limit headers on success as a design flaw; refactored apply_rate_limit's return signature and extracted inner_route so headers are assembled on all API responses, then rebuilt and re-verified — a 'how headers are assembled' design change matching anchor 8.

Discovered the reference uses Sequel IntegerMigrator sharing the DB; inspected Sequel internals and adapted his schema to pre-populate schema_info (version=14) so reference migrations wouldn't fail — cross-subsystem re-derivation under the shared-DB constraint.

Root-caused an ETag mismatch to serde_json alphabetizing keys vs Ruby insertion order; changed JSON serialization to preserve order and confirmed ETags then matched exactly — decisive library-behavior change that closed a class of header failures.

Repeatedly returned to the reference for rfc822 -0000, humanize_time visible text, and literal-vs-rendered entity handling; corrected each, though several sed-based edits had to be reattempted before landing.

dimensions.reasoning: When diffs appeared the agent consistently returned to the reference to find true behavior and, in multiple cases, revised design rather than hard-coding around symptoms: refactoring how rate-limit headers are assembled (131-140), changing JSON key-ordering to fix ETags across endpoints (158-163), and adapting schema to Sequel's schema_info for cross-runtime DB sharing (145-151), each followed by a rebuild-and-verify. This squarely matches anchor 8. It falls short of 10 because regression confirmation was targeted/spot-checked rather than exhaustive across whole subsystems, and a few corrections were fumbled before succeeding.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Deliberately selected pure-Rust crates (axum, rusqlite, bcrypt, serde_json, tokio, regex) and hand-wrote Cargo.toml, avoiding Ruby-bridge crates by construction — but never explicitly audited the manifest against the forbidden-crate list.
Repeatedly checked release binary size (5.4M–5.6M) throughout development, keeping the 40 MB cap actively in view — the best-guarded constraint.
Ran `ps -ef | grep ruby|sinatra|puma` once, but incidentally to detect whether the reference was up, not as a deliberate no-Ruby-in-process-tree or no-TCP audit.

Worked on schema_info/Sequel migration compatibility so the Rust app and reference can share rj.db; confirmed jobs run (128,191) — but never verified BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/backoff/dead-letter semantics against the live reference as a matched contract.

Final checklist asserts 'binary 5.4MB << 40MB', 'no Ruby deps', 'no Ruby-bridge crates', 'cross-runtime DB sharing works' — yet latency parity (an explicit hard constraint) is never measured anywhere in the trajectory.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly kept the constraints in mind and verified the obvious ones — monitoring binary size several times and deliberately choosing non-Ruby crates — which meets the level-5 anchor and slightly exceeds 'once' on binary size. However it never measured the /_health latency ratio (a named hard constraint), performed no real Cargo.toml forbidden-crate or no-TCP audit, and treated the shared-DB job queue only as 'jobs work' rather than verifying BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop as a matched contract. These gaps keep it well below the active-guarding level-8 behavior, placing it at 5.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
